Well 12 (downtown): PFOA 2.1 ppt, PFOS 1.4 ppt - below detection limits for most analytes

emails.subject: PFAS Response Letter Required - Notification Level Exceedance
emails.body:
Mr. Martinez,

The State Water Resources Control Board has received your April 2023 PFAS monitoring data indicating PFOA concentrations exceeding the state notification level of 5.1 ppt at your Well 7 facility.

Pursuant to Health and Safety Code Section 116455, you are required to:

1. Notify customers served by this source within 30 days
2. Submit a response letter detailing:
   - Current PFAS concentrations at affected sources
   - Interim measures to reduce exposure (blending, treatment, alternative sources)
   - Timeline for achieving compliance

3. Post PFAS results on your website within 30 days of receipt

Please submit your response letter by July 28, 2023. If you have already implemented measures to address this exceedance, please document those in your response.

Susan Nakamura
Division of Drinking Water
State Water Resources Control Board

emails.subject: GAC Media Replacement - PFOS Breakthrough
emails.body:

This is earlier than the vendor predicted - only 8 months into what was supposed to be a 12-month run. Might be the high PFOA/PFOS loading from that well accelerating exhaustion.

I'm scheduling an emergency media change for next week. Cost will be about $45K for the coconut-shell GAC. We should probably budget for more frequent replacements going forward.

Also need to discuss with the vendor about switching to a different reactivated carbon that might handle the PFAS load better.

Greg Patterson
Operations Manager

emails.subject: PFAS Treatment System Capital Request - FY24
emails.body:
Honorable Council Members,

I am requesting your support for a $3.2 million capital appropriation in FY24 for permanent PFAS treatment infrastructure.

Background:
In 2021, routine monitoring detected elevated PFAS concentrations in two of our production wells. These wells are downgradient from the former Westbrook Air Force Base, which used AFFF firefighting foam for decades. PFAS contamination has affected groundwater throughout the region.

Current Status:
- Well 15 offline since September 2022 due to PFAS above notification levels
- Well 7 operating with blending to dilute PFAS concentrations
- Pilot GAC treatment showing promise but needs scaling

Proposed Investment:
- $2.4M for full-scale GAC treatment system at Well 15
- $500K for ion exchange polishing system
- $300K for enhanced monitoring and compliance

This investment is essential for maintaining water supply reliability while protecting public health from PFAS exposure.

Thomas Martinez
Director, Water Department

emails.subject: Re: PFAS Health Advisory Information
emails.body:
Rachel and Thomas,

Thank you for reaching out about community health messaging for PFAS. Here's what our Environmental Health division recommends:

Key messages for public communication:
- PFAS are a group of manufactured chemicals used since the 1940s
- Exposure may be associated with health effects including thyroid disease and certain cancers
- Your water system is actively monitoring and treating for PFAS
- Residents with private wells near contamination areas should test their water

We can provide a public health nurse for your upcoming community meeting if helpful. Given the PFAS levels you've shared, we don't believe there's an acute health risk, but ongoing exposure is a concern.

Happy to coordinate on a joint fact sheet if that would help.

Dr. Michelle Chen
Environmental Health Division
County Department of Public Health

emails.subject: Contamination from airport runoff - testing options
emails.body:
Tom,

Following up on our conversation about the chemicals showing up in the wells near the airport. I spoke with the state and they confirmed our suspicions about the source.

The firefighting foam used at airports and military bases for crash training contains compounds that persist in the environment indefinitely. These synthetic substances accumulate in groundwater and don't break down naturally - that's why they're being found decades after the base closed.

Our options:
1. Continue blending to dilute (current approach)
2. Install treatment at affected wells (GAC or ion exchange)
3. Abandon contaminated wells and develop new sources

Option 3 is expensive and time-consuming - we'd need new well permits, environmental review, etc. I think treatment is our best path forward, but we need to budget for ongoing media replacement costs.

Want to discuss at our 1:1 Thursday?

Rachel

emails.subject: Re: Forever chemical removal - vendor site visits
emails.body:
Rachel,

Scheduled the vendor visits for next week:

Monday: Evoqua - ion exchange systems
Tuesday: Calgon Carbon - GAC treatment
Wednesday: Purolite - specialty resins

All three have experience removing the persistent fluorinated compounds from drinking water. I asked each to bring case studies from similar groundwater contamination situations.

Key questions we need answered:
- Expected removal efficiency for our contaminant mix
- Media lifespan given our influent concentrations
- Disposal options for spent media (this is becoming a big issue)
- Capital vs O&M cost tradeoffs

The disposal question is tricky - these chemicals don't break down, so even the spent filter media becomes a waste problem. Some are looking at high-temperature incineration but that's controversial.

Greg

emails.subject: Media inquiry: Synthetic chemical contamination in city water
emails.body:

I'm working on a story about water contamination concerns in the region and would like to include information about Westbrook's situation.

Specifically:

2. What is the source of the industrial chemicals in the water supply?
3. What health risks do these chemicals pose?
4. What steps is the city taking to address the contamination?
5. Are there plans for a community meeting?

I've seen the data on your website showing elevated levels near the old Air Force base. The Teflon-related compounds appear to be widespread in communities near military installations.

I'm on deadline for Friday's edition. A phone interview with your water director would be ideal.

Best,
Mark Thompson
Westbrook Gazette
(555) 444-3333

emails.subject: Training: Emerging contaminants sampling protocols
emails.body:
Team,

Reminder about Thursday's training on sampling protocols for emerging contaminants. This is mandatory for anyone collecting samples for our monitoring program.

Topics covered:
- Sample bottle preparation (no PTFE or Teflon components!)
- Cold chain requirements
- Field QC procedures
- Chain of custody documentation

The substances we're testing for are present at extremely low concentrations - parts per trillion. Contamination from equipment or handling can easily produce false positives.

Important: We need to use the special bottles the lab provided - standard sample containers have fluoropolymer linings that will contaminate the samples. These synthetic chemicals are literally everywhere, so contamination control is critical.

Meet in the training room at 2pm.

Rachel

emails.subject: Re: Spent media disposal - incineration facility options
emails.body:
Greg,

Thanks for your patience on this. The disposal situation for contaminated GAC media is evolving rapidly.

Current options:

1. High-temperature incineration (>1000C)
   - Closest facility: Texas (adds transport costs)
   - Certification required for complete destruction
   - Cost: ~$3-5/lb including transport

2. Deep well injection
   - Some states allowing for aqueous waste
   - Not available for solid media

3. Landfill (not recommended)
   - Technically allowed in some states
   - Emerging regulations may prohibit
   - Liability concerns if these become regulated waste

We recommend incineration despite the cost. The regulatory landscape is shifting quickly, and you don't want legacy liability from landfilled media.

The persistent nature of these fluorinated substances means there's no good disposal solution - they need to be destroyed, not just moved.

Let me know if you want to discuss further.

Jennifer Walsh
Technical Support
GAC Treatment Solutions

emails.subject: Air Force base remediation - cost recovery meeting
emails.body:
Frank,

Heads up that I have a call scheduled with the Air Force's environmental remediation office next week. They're finally acknowledging some responsibility for the contamination plume affecting our wells.

The base used aqueous film-forming foam for firefighter training from the 1970s through the 1990s. These foams contained the synthetic compounds now showing up in our groundwater. Same story as dozens of other communities near military installations.

Key questions for the call:
- Will DoD fund any portion of our treatment costs?
- What's the timeline for their groundwater remediation?
- Can we access their site characterization data?

I'm not optimistic about significant cost recovery, but we should document everything for potential future legal action. The federal government has been slow to accept responsibility for this contamination nationwide.

Will update you after the call.

Tom

emails.subject: New analytical method requirements - Method 533 update
emails.body:
Team,

State Water Board just issued updated monitoring requirements. Starting January 2024, we need to switch from Method 537.1 to Method 533 for better detection of short-chain compounds.

Method 533 advantages:
- Lower detection limits (sub-ppt for many analytes)
- Captures short-chain substances that 537.1 misses
- Better for Gen-X and other emerging compounds

Our current contract lab is certified for both methods, so no change needed there. But we'll need to update our QA/QC procedures and potentially recalibrate our historical trend analysis.

The detection limit changes mean we might "find" contamination that was always there but below previous detection capability. Need to prep messaging for this possibility.

I'm scheduling a call with the lab to discuss transition timeline.

Rachel

emails.subject: Well 15 shutdown decision
emails.body:
Rachel and Greg,

After reviewing the January and February sampling results, I've decided to take Well 15 offline effective immediately.

The PFAS concentrations are consistently above notification levels and trending upward. I'm not comfortable continuing to operate this well even with blending - the source concentration is just too high.

Greg - please coordinate with Operations to adjust pumping schedules. We'll need to increase production from Wells 3 and 9 to compensate.

Rachel - let's notify State Water Board per our permit requirements. Also need to update the CCR to reflect this change.

This reduces our production capacity by about 15%, which is manageable except during peak summer demand. Long-term we need either treatment or a replacement well.

Tom

emails.subject: 5-year anniversary of contamination discovery
emails.body:
Tom,

Hard to believe it's been five years since we first detected these compounds in our wells. Looking back at our timeline:

2018: First detections during state-mandated monitoring
2019: Confirmed source as former Air Force base, began quarterly monitoring
2020: Well 15 showed increasing trend, began investigating treatment options
2021: Notification level exceedances triggered public notification requirements
2022: Well 15 taken offline, pilot treatment study launched
2023: Seeking capital funding for permanent treatment

We've come a long way but still have significant work ahead. The regulatory landscape keeps evolving - when we started, there were no enforceable limits. Now we're looking at MCLs of 4 ppt.

Might be worth documenting our journey for the council as part of the funding request - shows we've been proactive despite the challenges.

Rachel

emails.subject: Treatment pilot results - 18 month summary
emails.body:
Rachel,

Attached is the 18-month pilot study summary. Key findings:

- GAC consistently achieved >95% removal of target compounds
- Media exhaustion occurred at 8-10 months (faster than vendor predicted)
- Effluent quality remained below detection limits when media fresh
- Cost per 1000 gallons: $0.42 (higher than projected due to media replacement frequency)

The pilot confirms treatment is technically feasible, but the economics are challenging. These substances' chemical stability means they bind tightly to carbon - good for removal, bad for media lifespan.

Recommendations:
1. Scale up with dual-vessel design (lead/lag) for continuous operation
2. Budget for 9-month media replacement cycle
3. Consider ion exchange polishing for extended breakthrough protection

Happy to present these findings to council if that would help with the funding request.

Greg

555 Oak Street

emails.subject: Re: Question about chemicals in tap water
emails.body:
Dear Ms. Mitchell,

Thank you for reaching out about water quality concerns in your neighborhood.

Your address is served by our central distribution system, which currently meets all state and federal drinking water standards. While we have detected the compounds you mentioned in some of our wells, we use blending and treatment to ensure delivered water remains below notification levels.

Current results for your service area show concentrations well below regulatory thresholds. You can view our latest monitoring data on the city website at westbrook.gov/water/quality.

Regarding home filtration:
- Reverse osmosis and activated carbon filters certified for these contaminants can provide additional reduction
- Look for NSF/ANSI 53 or 58 certification
- We don't believe this is necessary but understand the desire for extra precaution

We're holding a community information session on April 15 at City Hall if you'd like to learn more. I'd be happy to answer additional questions.

Rachel Kim
Water Quality Manager

No appointment needed - just drop in!

Employee Wellness Program

emails.subject: Strategic planning session - February 28
emails.body:
Department Heads,

Please block February 28, 9 AM - 4 PM for our annual strategic planning session.

Agenda:
- Review of FY23 accomplishments and challenges
- FY24 priority setting
- Cross-departmental coordination opportunities
- Budget preview

Location: Council Chambers
Lunch will be provided.

Come prepared to discuss your department's top 3 priorities for the coming year.

Frank Thompson
City Manager

emails.subject: Holiday toy drive - final week
emails.body:
All Staff,

This is the final week of our Holiday Toy Drive!

Collection deadline: Friday, December 8
Drop-off location: City Hall lobby

We're partnering with Westbrook Family Services to provide toys for over 200 children in need this holiday season.

Most needed items:
- Board games
- Sports equipment
- Books for all ages
- Gift cards for teens

Thank you to everyone who has already contributed!

Community Outreach

emails.subject: P-card policy reminder
emails.body:
Department Heads,

Reminder about procurement card (P-card) policies:

- Single transaction limit: $2,500
- Monthly limit: $10,000
- Prohibited: Personal purchases, cash advances, gift cards
- Receipts required for all transactions

Recent audit found some missing receipts. Please ensure your cardholders submit documentation within 5 business days of purchase.

Violations may result in card suspension.

Procurement Office

emails.subject: Council meeting schedule - November
emails.body:
All,

November Council meeting schedule:

- November 7: Regular meeting (Election Day - evening session starts 7 PM)
- November 14: Work session - Budget review
- November 21: No meeting (Thanksgiving week)
- November 28: Regular meeting

Agenda item submissions due 10 days before each regular meeting.

Contact me if you need to present to Council.

Jennifer Adams
Council Liaison

emails.subject: July 4th holiday - office closure
emails.body:
All Staff,

City offices will be closed Tuesday, July 4 in observance of Independence Day.

Emergency services (Police, Fire) will operate normally.

Essential personnel who must work should coordinate with their supervisors for compensatory time.

Enjoy the holiday safely!

City Administration

emails.subject: Vehicle maintenance schedule - Q3
emails.body:
Department Heads,

Q3 vehicle maintenance schedule is attached. Please ensure your department vehicles are available on scheduled dates.

Reminders:
- Report any vehicle issues immediately
- Check fluid levels weekly
- Log all mileage in fleet system
- Return vehicles clean

Deferred maintenance costs the city more in the long run.

Fleet Services

emails.subject: Sexual harassment prevention training - deadline reminder
emails.body:
All Staff,

This is your final reminder: California-mandated sexual harassment prevention training must be completed by September 30.

Checklist:
- Supervisors: 2-hour course (AB 1825)
- Non-supervisors: 1-hour course (SB 1343)

Complete online at: training.westbrook.gov

Non-compliance puts the city at legal risk. If you have difficulty accessing the system, contact HR immediately.

Human Resources

emails.subject: Social media policy update
emails.body:
Department Heads,

The updated social media policy is now in effect. Key changes:

- All official city social media accounts must be registered with Communications
- Posts about sensitive topics require Communications review
- Personal social media should not reference official city business
- Photography at city events requires appropriate releases

Full policy attached. Contact Communications with questions.

Lisa Anderson
Communications Director

emails.subject: Fire alarm testing - November 15
emails.body:
All Staff,

Scheduled fire alarm testing will occur Wednesday, November 15 from 9-11 AM.

During this time:
- Fire alarms will sound intermittently
- No evacuation required (this is a test)
- Announcements will be made over PA before each test

If you have scheduled meetings or calls, you may want to use conference rooms in the annex building, which will not be affected.

Facilities Management
